cortical: Figure 1. Mature neuronal populations differ in how closely their exon usage resembles that of mature cortex. Panels a and b show exon inclusion fractions at nine ages in mouse cortex and eight in frontal cortex. Corresponding rows show the same exon event. The 2,883 events are grouped by published module (M1–M4 contain 1,118, 1,027, 385 and 353 events), then sorted by first-age inclusion in panel a. Pale grey marks the 1,277 missing event-by-age values. E, embryonic day. P, postnatal day. For panel c we calculated the median and interquartile range of late minus early inclusion within each exon, using the 2,577 events with both endpoints measured in both series (M1–M4: 979, 938, 336, 324). The intervals describe differences across exons. Panel d gives sample counts by the authors’ overall inferred splicing stage. Blank cells indicate zero samples. All 16 samples have chronological stage 6 in the source. Replotted from supplementary datasets S5 and S8b [@Weyn2018].
robo: Figure 2. ROBO microexon deletions alter early commissure thickness and midline crossing. Panel a shows alternative paths through exon 6b. Arcs represent connectivity. Panel b shows the E12.5 contralateral-to-ipsilateral DiI signal ratio relative to wild type. In b, an edit denotes deletion of one copy of exon 6b at the indicated locus in Nova1/2 double-knockout mice. Panel c shows early lumbar ROBO3-positive commissure thickness divided by floor-plate thickness at E10.5. Here exon deletions are homozygous and NOVA is intact. Points and bars show the published means and standard deviations. The two workbooks use different SD conventions (sample SD in b, population SD in c). Embryo counts give the number of animals per group. Reading counts give the number of individual measurements. The workbooks do not identify which measurements came from the same embryo. Replotted from source data for figures 4C and 7D [@Johnson2019].
routes: Figure 3. Four mechanisms link RNA processing to protein production or function. In panel a, a cue from the floor plate permits commissural axons to translate stored *Robo3.2* RNA bearing retained intron 26. Translation also exposes that RNA to nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) [@Chen2008;@Colak2013]. In panel b, alternative transcription initiation in myocardium can preserve RBM20 activity. RBM20 regulates inclusion of titin spring exons. Inclusion of more spring sequence produces a longer extensible region. The transcription-start schematic, spring lengths and arrows are qualitative. The passive-tension comparison comes from developing rat cardiomyocytes [@Guo2012RBM20;@Radke2026;@Opitz2004]. In panel c, inclusion of the *Tra2b* poison exon limits TRA2B abundance in germ cells and thereby influences downstream splicing [@Dalgliesh2025]. Panel d shows how astrocytes in the postnatal mouse subventricular zone supply soluble DLK1. In a separate rescue, restoring the membrane form to deficient stem cells enabled soluble DLK1 to stimulate neurosphere formation. Arrows show the requirements identified by separate rescue experiments [@Ferron2011].
snap25: Figure 4. Replacing SNAP-25b with SNAP-25a alters total SNAP-25 abundance differently in two mouse lines. The lines retain or lack the selection cassette used in allele construction. Panel a shows the exon-5a share of total Snap25a plus Snap25b RNA in mouse brain on postnatal day 14 (five mice per genotype). Wild-type points are littermate controls for the corresponding line. Panel b shows total RNA and protein in homozygous mice at postnatal day 14 (RNA) or days 14–15 (protein) relative to each line's wild-type littermates (six mice per genotype). Points and error bars show published means and standard errors. At 100%, the authors report exclusive 5a expression without a numerical standard error. The wild-type reference in b is 100% by normalisation. Data transcribed from figures 1B–D and 2B–D of Johansson et al. [@Johansson2008].
timing: Figure 6. Two developmental histories give the same transient difference between regions. Gounder and Hamilton assessed transient divergence across developing brain regions [@GounderHamilton2026]. The curves here are constructed examples of transcript A as a fraction of two products from one gene. Transcript B accounts for the remainder. In panel a both regions undergo replacement at different ages and retain the later state through the final observation. In panel b, the fraction rises briefly in one region and remains constant in the other. Lines connect successive constructed values. Each lower plot shows the absolute difference between the regions above it. The absolute between-region differences at the five ages are 0, 0, 0.6, 0 and 0 in both panels. The fractions in the upper panels distinguish sustained replacement in both regions from a temporary change in one.
fruitless: Figure 5. Timed perturbations identify a developmental requirement in flies and advance cell fusion in nematodes. In panels a and b, each column represents a cohort in which FruM knockdown was induced for two days beginning at the indicated stage. Panel a shows the courtship index for each of 24 males per cohort. Horizontal bars mark medians. Dots are spread horizontally to resolve individuals at similar values. Panel b shows how many of the 24 males mated. Filled squares denote males that mated. Positions in the two panels do not link individual flies. Stage 5 coincides with pupation. The scheduled knockdown window is distinct from the duration of protein depletion. Replotted from the source data for figure 1C,D of Chen et al. [@Chen2021Fru]. Panel c marks the larval stages at which seam cells fuse under normal conditions and after early epidermal expression of LIN-29a or LIN-29b. Gonad morphology independently confirmed the early L2 stage. Symbols indicate observed stages, with no estimate of elapsed time between them [@Azzi2020].
